name: B12 booster shots

lead:
B12 booster shots are injections (or IV drips) of vitamin B12 given at clinics and wellness spas. People take them for energy and well-being, and in people with low B12 correcting the shortfall can address fatigue and pale skin.
In medicine, injections are the standard first treatment for more serious deficiency, followed by lower maintenance doses. Forum users in the TRT and supplement communities also mention B12 shots as an add-on.

paras: Clinics give the shots intramuscularly, usually after or alongside blood testing. Deficiency treatment typically starts with higher doses and moves to maintenance by injection or by mouth.

Reported injection side effects include skin rash, itching, chills, fever, hot flushes, nausea and dizziness. No upper intake level has been set because no adverse effects from high doses have been documented in humans.

angle.text: In people with low B12, injections correct the deficiency behind fatigue and pallor. People without deficiency take them for energy, a use that has not been tested.

lead: B12 booster shots are injections or intravenous infusions of vitamin B12 marketed for energy and wellness. In deficiency, which can cause anaemia, tiredness, pale skin, a sore tongue and nerve symptoms, replacing B12 treats those symptoms [1].

The appearance angle runs through correction of deficiency: restoring B12 addresses the paleness and fatigue and the lack of motivation to exercise associated with anaemia [1]. B12 injections are the recognised first treatment for more serious deficiency, followed by lower maintenance doses by injection or mouth [1][2].

People most at risk include those with pernicious anaemia, stomach surgery, Crohn's or coeliac disease, long-term acid-reducing drug or metformin use, and low animal food intake [1]. In forums such as T Nation, men on testosterone therapy and those discussing low T mention B12 shots as a supplement, and some users judge them modest in effect [3].

paras: Severe deficiency requires injections initially, with high early doses followed by maintenance, by mouth or injection; a 2019 study cited suggests oral B12 is inferior in severe cases [1]. Daily intramuscular injections are the standard initial treatment, then monthly injections or daily oral doses [2].

Reported injection side effects include skin rash, itching, chills, fever, hot flushes, nausea and dizziness [2]. No tolerable upper intake level has been set in the US or EU, since no human data show adverse effects from high doses [2].
Users on T Nation mention B12 shots alongside TRT and low-testosterone discussions, with one writer calling them not very effective but better than nothing [3].
No studies found specific to booster shots in people without deficiency. Studies of deficiency treatment compare oral and intramuscular B12 [1].
